tagline: Up through the Cookson Hills to Tahlequah and the Illinois River.
intro: North of I-40 the byway takes Highway 10 to Gore, which calls itself the trout capital of Oklahoma, then follows Highways 100 and 82 past Lake Tenkiller and through the Cookson Hills, by Cookson and Keys, into Tahlequah. Beyond town Highway 10 keeps to the Illinois River under sheer cliff faces before turning east for the Arkansas line, 84 miles from the start.

Tahlequah has been a Cherokee capital since 1839, when the Nation rebuilt itself at the end of the Trail of Tears. An earlier one, Tahlonteeskee, capital of the Western Cherokee from 1828, stood two miles north of Gore.

moments.title: Lake Tenkiller
moments.text: The Illinois River backed up behind an earth dam finished in 1952, named for the Tenkiller family, Cherokees whose land and ferry were bought to make room for it.

moments.title: Cherokee National Capitol
moments.text: Built from 1867 to 1869, after the Civil War had wrecked most of Tahlequah's public buildings, it housed the Cherokee Nation's government until statehood in 1907. It is a history museum now.

moments.title: Natural Falls
moments.text: A 77-foot fall into a narrow valley, the water cooling about ten degrees on the way down. Until 1990 it was a private roadside stop called Dripping Springs.
